reasoning_traces.think:
The foundational principle of substitutability arises from the assumption that identity is rooted in shared essential properties. If two entities share the same fundamental essence, they are logically indistinguishable in any proposition. This leads to a radical form of justice where moral and legal equivalences are derived from such commonality. The radicality of this justice increases with the simplicity and fundamentality of the essence considered. Abstract reasoning, while powerful, risks losing the individuality of cases, whereas instinctive perception preserves uniqueness but may lack generality. The tension between these two modes of reasoning constitutes the core of human deliberation. In GSI, this manifests as Bayesian updating over relational structures, where prior beliefs are adjusted based on shared essences. In GSE, it translates into state transitions that balance formal logic with experiential nuance. The failure mode occurs when either abstraction or concreteness dominates without integration, leading to either mechanical justice or arbitrary intuition.
